paper.title: ThermalSplat: Generalizable Pose-Free Gaussian Splatting for Sparse-View Thermal 3D Reconstruction
paper.summary: Thermal infrared imaging is vital for applications like search-and-rescue and autonomous navigation, yet trans- lating it into 3D scene representations remains a critical bottleneck. The low-texture nature and view-dependent emissivity of thermal images cause standard pose estima- tors to fail catastrophically, collapsing standard 3D Gaus- sian Splatting pipelines under sparse-view constraints. Fur- thermore, existing thermal reconstruction methods rely heavily on dense capture and computationally expensive per-scene optimization. Critically, many of these ap- proaches depend on aligned RGB-thermal datasets to ob- tain reliable camera poses and initial point clouds, ren- dering them unusable in purely thermal, unposed envi- ronments. To break this bottleneck, we present Thermal- Splat, the first generalizable, feed-forward Gaussian splat- ting framework that reconstructs 3D scenes directly from sparse thermal images without requiring known camera poses, RGB guidance, or per-scene training. We over- come thermal-specific challenges using a soft census loss for brightness-invariant structural matching and a bound- ary structure loss to explicitly supervise temperature discon- tinuities. Trained on an aggregated multi-source dataset, ThermalSplat synthesizes sharp reconstructions of unseen scenes in a single feed-forward pass. Extensive experi- ments demonstrate that ThermalSplat holds a strict advan- tage over scene-specific thermal splatting methods in the sparse regime. Furthermore, even compared against these baselines operating under their ideal dense capture set- tings, ThermalSplat achieves superior perceptual fidelity. By eliminating the need for computationally expensive per scene optimization, ThermalSplat offers an efficient and generalizable approach to thermal 3D reconstruction.

analysis.problem_statement: Standard 3D Gaussian Splatting pipelines fail on thermal infrared images due to low texture and pose estimation failures, necessitating a method that reconstructs 3D scenes from sparse, unposed thermal data without RGB guidance or per-scene optimization.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: The lack of generalizable, feed-forward 3D reconstruction methods for low-texture, pose-free thermal imagery, which currently relies on computationally expensive per-scene optimization and dense capture.
analysis.executive_summary: ThermalSplat addresses the critical gap in thermal 3D reconstruction by eliminating the dependency on accurate camera poses and RGB-thermal alignment, which are often unavailable in real-world search-and-rescue or autonomous navigation scenarios. By introducing a generalizable feed-forward framework, it enables efficient, single-pass reconstruction of unseen scenes from sparse thermal views, significantly reducing computational overhead compared to traditional per-scene optimization methods.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Superior perceptual fidelity and reconstruction quality in sparse-view regimes compared to scene-specific baselines, even when those baselines operate under ideal dense capture settings.
key_metrics.baseline: Scene-specific thermal splatting methods (both sparse and dense capture settings)

technical_breakdown.method: A generalizable, feed-forward Gaussian splatting framework that directly reconstructs 3D scenes from sparse thermal images without known camera poses, RGB guidance, or per-scene training.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Feed-forward neural network architecture designed for pose-free Gaussian Splatting, incorporating specific loss functions to handle thermal image characteristics.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Utilizes a 'soft census loss' for brightness-invariant structural matching and a 'boundary structure loss' to explicitly supervise temperature discontinuities. Trained on an aggregated multi-source dataset to ensure generalization to unseen scenes.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Eliminates computationally expensive per-scene optimization, enabling reconstruction in a single feed-forward pass, which implies significantly lower inference latency and computational cost compared to iterative optimization methods.

paper.title: Honest Fusion Evaluation for Cross-Domain Deepfake Detection: Leakage Audits and Tail Robustness
paper.summary: Cross-domain video deepfake detection increasingly uses frozen foundation-model experts, combined by calibrated score averaging, a per-video router picking one expert, or a learned head over concatenated features. Expressive routing and feature fusion are often reported to beat plain averaging. Across a 22-dataset frozen-expert testbed, we find those gains are largely evaluation artifacts. A corner theorem locates the gap routing aims to close: because AUC depends only on score ordering, the best any score-space router can do is an oracle reading the test label to pick each video's expert, a ceiling no realisable, label-blind router reaches. The theorem does not order real routers against a calibrated global average; the case against routing is empirical, and no router we test beats that average. Feature fusion reads raw features, falls outside the theorem, and is audited empirically. Reported gains trace to leakage: holding out one dataset leaks siblings sharing identities and reals (over-crediting routing), while holding out one manipulation keeps that dataset's reals in training (over-crediting feature fusion). A $2\times 2$ over fold and evaluation granularity pins the $+2.6$pp feature-fusion "win" to the fold alone: 12/12 significant under leaky folds vs. 0/12 under honest family-held-out folds, where both gains vanish. Fusion still pays off in the tail of hard videos and families: as experts are added, videos every expert misclassifies drop from 15.2% to 2.3%, and global calibrated fusion (InvB) beats the best single expert on worst-family AUC, selective risk (AURC), and low-false-positive recall, stably across protocols. Practitioners should calibrate and combine globally, hold out whole dataset families, and measure tail performance. For score-space routing under ranking metrics, honest evaluation and expert diversity matter more than combiner complexity.

analysis.executive_summary: This work demonstrates that expressive routing and feature fusion methods for deepfake detection do not outperform simple calibrated score averaging when evaluated with honest, family-held-out protocols. It identifies specific leakage mechanisms where shared identities or real videos across datasets artificially inflate the performance of complex combiners, providing a rigorous framework for fair evaluation in the field.

They use a 2x2 analysis over fold and evaluation granularity to isolate leakage effects, demonstrating that gains vanish when whole dataset families are held out.

technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Low computational overhead for the evaluation framework itself, as it relies on frozen experts; the focus is on rigorous data partitioning and statistical auditing rather than heavy model training.

paper.title: Paired Geometric Supervision for Generalizable Deepfake Detection
paper.summary: We present OrthoPairGTL, a geometric training framework for cross-domain deepfake detection, built on a partially frozen DINOv3 backbone ($\sim$300M parameters), and make three contributions: (1) We re-evaluate six recent transfer-learning detectors (Forensics Adapter, Effort, three GenD variants and FakeSTormer) using the authors' released checkpoints under a single preprocessing pipeline across 17 cross-domain datasets (2018-2025), so that the reported gaps reflect method rather than per-method pipeline tuning. (2) We model the transformation between paired real and fake samples, training Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) adapters with an orthogonal pair decomposition, hyperspherical regularisation, and (in the GSD-LoRA variant) a set-level coherence objective. (3) Under LoRA, this regularisation gives a more stable optimisation profile: GSD-LoRA's post-peak validation degradation is $4.2\times$ shallower than plain LoRA at the same parameter footprint, and the time-averaged validation AUC across training is 1.82 pp higher. On the 17 datasets, GSD-LoRA matches or exceeds every re-evaluated baseline (92.82% vs. 91.58% for the strongest; paired Wilcoxon signed-rank $p=0.015$, 13/17 per-dataset wins), with the largest gains on modern reenactment-heavy benchmarks (DSv1.1, DSv2). Under strict parameter budgets, LayerNorm-only tuning ($\approx$0.03% of the backbone) is the most stable configuration and matches the strongest baseline with a mean of 91.97%.

analysis.executive_summary: This work provides a rigorous re-evaluation of recent transfer-learning detectors under a unified pipeline, highlighting that previous performance gaps may be attributed to pipeline tuning rather than methodological superiority. It introduces OrthoPairGTL, a geometric training framework that leverages paired real-fake samples to improve optimization stability and cross-domain performance. The results demonstrate that specific regularization techniques can significantly enhance the generalizability of large vision transformers for deepfake detection without requiring full model fine-tuning.

It models the transformation between paired real and fake samples using an orthogonal pair decomposition and hyperspherical regularization. A set-level coherence objective is added in the GSD-LoRA variant to ensure stability.

technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Key techniques include orthogonal pair decomposition, hyperspherical regularization, and a set-level coherence objective. technical_breakdown.code_complexity: The method is parameter-efficient, with LayerNorm-only tuning using approximately 0.03% of the backbone parameters. GSD-LoRA offers a more stable optimization profile with 4.2x shallower post-peak validation degradation compared to plain LoRA.

paper.title: Breath-Dx: A Time Series Classification Benchmark for Disease Screening with eNose
paper.summary: Electronic nose (eNose) technology offers a portable, non-invasive route for disease screening via exhaled breath analysis. However, progress in the field is hindered by the lack of systematic benchmarks that compare machine learning methods under realistic conditions, particularly sensor drift, a known but rarely quantified failure mode. Most existing studies rely on small, private datasets with inconsistent protocols, rendering results non-comparable and slowing progress. We introduce Breath-Dx, the first comprehensive benchmark of time series classification methods for breath-based disease screening. Our work leverages the Scent of Health (S-OH) dataset, the largest public clinical eNose collection to date, comprising 1,234 patients across nine diagnostic groups, each providing a 17-channel multivariate time series with explicit temporal train/test splits that account for sensor drift. We systematically evaluate 10 methods spanning four families: feature-based tabular learners, convolution-based models, graph-based, and time series architectures. All methods degrade significantly under temporal validation (0.05-0.12 AUC drop compared to random cross-validation), confirming that drift embeds a strong temporal signal. Under this realistic evaluation, the best methods achieve ROC AUC of 0.74-0.76 for some lung conditions, though others remain near chance. Recurrent architectures show the most consistent performance across diseases, while specialized time series methods achieve the highest peak results. Demographic confounders matter: breath signals provide independent diagnostic value for some conditions but add little beyond age for others. We release the S-OH dataset, all temporal splits, evaluation protocols, and code to enable reproducible research and accelerate progress in clinical breathomics.

analysis.executive_summary: This paper establishes the first comprehensive benchmark for breath-based disease screening using the large-scale Scent of Health dataset, highlighting that standard random cross-validation overestimates performance by ignoring sensor drift. It demonstrates that realistic temporal validation reveals significant performance degradation, providing a crucial baseline for developing robust clinical eNose applications.

paper.title: SecDVA: A Maliciously Secure Multi-Party Framework for Data Value Assessment in Modern Machine Learning Data Markets
paper.summary: Data Value Assessment (DVA) plays a critical role in modern data markets by enabling buyers to evaluate how a seller's data would improve model performance before purchase. However, existing DVA approaches require one party to reveal the data or model, exposing participants to privacy leakage, strategic manipulation, and high deployment costs. These limitations motivate a DVA protocol that is secure, reliable, widely applicable, and efficient enough for practical deployment in modern data markets. In this paper, we present SecDVA, the first maliciously secure multi-party computation (MPC) framework for reliable and practical DVA in modern machine learning data markets. SecDVA ensures that neither the seller's data nor the buyer's model and test data are disclosed beyond the final DVA outcome, while remaining robust against malicious behavior. To address the efficiency and applicability challenges of DVA for large models, we use the neural tangent kernel theory to linearize model updates and introduce lightweight mini-batch approximations to significantly reduce computation overhead. We further design a (2+1)-party MPC protocol based on function secret sharing, together with optimized non-linear primitives. In addition, we optimize the underlying MPC backends, the distributed point function, and the distributed comparison function, reducing the number of Advanced Encryption Standard calls to improve efficiency. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SecDVA outperforms existing baselines in the plaintext setting and enables DVA for large-scale models in a reasonable time under MPC.

analysis.problem_statement: Existing Data Value Assessment (DVA) protocols in machine learning data markets lack malicious security, forcing participants to reveal sensitive data or models, which exposes them to privacy leakage and strategic manipulation.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Privacy-preserving data valuation and secure multi-party computation efficiency for large-scale model evaluation.
analysis.executive_summary: SecDVA addresses the critical gap in secure data trading by providing the first maliciously secure MPC framework for Data Value Assessment. It enables buyers to evaluate the utility of seller data without exposing either party's private assets, facilitating trustworthy and efficient transactions in modern ML data markets.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Efficiency of MPC-based DVA for large-scale models compared to plaintext baselines and existing MPC methods
key_metrics.baseline: Existing DVA baselines in plaintext setting and prior MPC approaches

technical_breakdown.method: The framework utilizes Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) theory to linearize model updates, allowing for lightweight mini-batch approximations that reduce computational overhead. It employs a (2+1)-party MPC protocol based on Function Secret Sharing (FSS) to ensure security against malicious adversaries.
technical_breakdown.architecture: A (2+1)-party Multi-Party Computation architecture involving a seller, a buyer, and a helper/server, utilizing optimized non-linear primitives and distributed functions.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Key techniques include NTK-based linearization, mini-batch approximations, Function Secret Sharing (FSS), and optimized implementations of Distributed Point Function (DPF) and Distributed Comparison Function (DCF) to minimize AES calls.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Significantly reduced computation overhead for large models via linearization and mini-batching; optimized backend reduces cryptographic primitive calls (AES) to improve practical deployment speed.

paper.title: Transactional Data Change for Real-Time Analytics in Lakehouses
paper.summary: Real-time data analytics has become a key demand for lakehouses. It requires propagating data changes from the data source to the lakehouse in real time, while ensuring ACID guarantees and minimizing resource consumption and impact on analytical query performance. This is highly challenging for a data system according to the RUM conjecture, especially given the read-optimized immutable file storage layer in lakehouses. Existing lakehouses offer only git-style catalog version control on a single table, and they trade data freshness, query performance, and/or resource efficiency to achieve a barely acceptable data-change throughput. In this paper, we propose a novel data synchronization framework, Retina, that enables real-time, cost-efficient, query-performant, and fully transactional data changes in lakehouses. We implement and open-source Retina. Evaluations show that Retina delivers 10-millisecond-level data freshness and over 3.2 million row/s linear-scalable data-change throughput with low resource consumption and query-performance overhead, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art lakehouse systems and lake-compatible HTAP databases.

analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the critical gap in lakehouse architectures where real-time data ingestion conflicts with read-optimized immutable storage, typically forcing trade-offs between freshness, performance, and cost. By introducing Retina, a novel synchronization framework, it enables millisecond-level data freshness and high-throughput transactional changes while maintaining low overhead for analytical queries. This is significant for the AI landscape as it facilitates the ingestion of high-velocity data streams required for real-time model inference and feedback loops within unified data platforms.

paper.title: EASTAR: Event-Anchored Semantic and Task-Adaptive Region Representation Learning
paper.summary: Urban region representation learning supports a wide range of urban analytics tasks by encoding regional functions and interactions, with human mobility serving as a central signal because it directly captures inter-region interactions. However, most mobility-based methods learn from aggregated origin-destination matrices, where trips driven by different activity purposes are mixed into purpose-agnostic interaction patterns. Although static urban attributes such as POIs and land use can enrich region-level semantics, they do not explicitly ground mobility interactions in activity-purpose signals. As a result, downstream adaptation is often performed over entangled embeddings, making it difficult to select task-relevant functional semantics. To address these limitations, we propose EASTAR, an event-anchored and task-adaptive framework for urban region representation learning. EASTAR treats offline activity events as sparse semantic anchors and uses them to factorize aggregated mobility representations into multiple purpose-related semantic channels. It further introduces free channels to capture latent mobility patterns not covered by event data and a global channel to preserve overall spatial structure. To adapt the learned channel space to different downstream objectives, EASTAR designs a task-adaptive prompt router that initializes task-channel relevance from LLM-derived priors and refines the routing weights through downstream supervision. Experiments on two real-world urban datasets across four prediction tasks show that EASTAR consistently outperforms representative baselines, achieving up to 39.15% reduction in MAE. Ablation and interpretability analyses further demonstrate the effectiveness of event anchoring, semantic channel construction, and task-adaptive routing.

analysis.executive_summary: This work addresses the limitation of purpose-agnostic mobility models by introducing a framework that uses offline activity events as semantic anchors to factorize regional representations into distinct purpose-related channels. By incorporating a task-adaptive prompt router initialized with LLM priors, the method enables more precise selection of relevant functional semantics for downstream urban analytics tasks.

paper.title: CuEVM: Scaling Smart Contract Execution on GPUs
paper.summary: Smart contracts on Ethereum blockchain process transactions worth billions of US dollars daily. They run on top of Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) which executes transactions sequentially. This execution model creates a performance bottleneck, especially for new blockchain workloads with large numbers of transactions, such as security testing. We present CuEVM, a GPU-native and semantically complete EVM execution engine that treats transaction execution as a massively parallel data processing problem. It employs novel data structures and GPU-aware scheduling to accelerate execution. Unlike prior works that transpile the contract and rely on a host CPU for many operations, CuEVM supports complete EVM semantics natively on the GPU. It passes 100% of the Ethereum VMTests and 96.2% of the full execution-test suite. On a single commodity GPU, CuEVM executes over 8 million ERC-20 transfers per second, outperforming existing baselines by up to two orders of magnitude. We build a smart contract fuzzer, called CuEVM-fuzz, on top of CuEVM. The fuzzer achieves over a million end-to-end executions per second, up to 23x and 4.8x higher than the state-of-the-art CPU-based and GPU-based baselines, respectively.

analysis.executive_summary: CuEVM addresses the scalability limits of blockchain infrastructure by treating transaction execution as a massively parallel data processing problem on GPUs. By achieving native, semantically complete EVM execution without relying on host CPU transpilation, it enables high-frequency security testing and transaction validation at scales previously impossible with CPU-based or hybrid approaches.

paper.title: Observations Drift, Structures Remain: Structural Pretraining with Time Alignment for Electromagnetic Signals
paper.summary: Electromagnetic signal modeling is increasingly moving toward self-supervised pretraining on heterogeneous I/Q observations. However, an observed waveform is jointly shaped by signal generation, propagation environments, and acquisition processes, which mix reusable structural regularities with observation-specific variations. Existing methods usually pursue unified pretraining with reconstruction objectives on mixed observations. This heterogeneity creates two key mismatches for reconstruction pretraining: (1) appearance mismatch, induced by propagation-dependent waveform variations; and (2) temporal mismatch, induced by acquisition-dependent sampling coordinates. These mismatches make observation-specific appearances and sampling coordinates easier to reconstruct than stable signal structures, inducing observational shortcuts. We identify this failure mode as observation-biased pretraining. To address this, we propose Structural Pretraining with Time Alignment for heterogeneous EM signals. It mitigates temporal mismatch with RoPE-fs, which maps token positions to sampling-rate-normalized physical-time positions, and reduces reliance on appearance shortcuts by replacing waveform reconstruction with masked prediction of discrete structural units. These units are organized into atomic structural units and emergent structural units that capture variable-length compositional patterns beyond fixed patch boundaries. Across diverse EM benchmarks, our method improves both full-supervision and few-shot adaptation over existing EM pretraining baselines, showing that the learned representations better preserve structural consistency when observations drift in waveform appearance and temporal scale.

analysis.problem_statement: The paper addresses the issue of 'observation-biased pretraining' in electromagnetic (EM) signal modeling, where reconstruction objectives on heterogeneous I/Q data lead models to learn observation-specific shortcuts (appearance and temporal mismatches) rather than stable, reusable signal structures.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Generalization gap in self-supervised learning for non-stationary, heterogeneous sensor data due to distribution shift in acquisition and propagation conditions.
analysis.executive_summary: This work is significant because it shifts EM signal pretraining from pixel/waveform-level reconstruction to structure-level prediction, effectively decoupling invariant signal features from variable environmental and acquisition artifacts. By introducing time-aligned positional encoding and discrete structural units, it enables robust few-shot adaptation and full-supervision performance across diverse benchmarks, addressing a critical limitation in current self-supervised approaches for physical signal processing.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Improvement in full-supervision and few-shot adaptation accuracy over existing EM pretraining baselines.
key_metrics.baseline: Existing EM pretraining baselines (reconstruction-based methods)

technical_breakdown.method: The proposed method, Structural Pretraining with Time Alignment, replaces waveform reconstruction with masked prediction of discrete structural units. It uses RoPE-fs to map token positions to sampling-rate-normalized physical-time positions to mitigate temporal mismatch, and organizes structural units into atomic and emergent categories to capture variable-length compositional patterns.
technical_breakdown.architecture: A transformer-based architecture (implied by RoPE usage) that processes I/Q observations, utilizing a modified positional encoding scheme (RoPE-fs) and a discrete structural unit prediction head instead of a continuous reconstruction head.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Key techniques include: 1) RoPE-fs (Rotary Position Embedding with sampling-rate normalization) to align temporal coordinates; 2) Masked prediction of discrete structural units (atomic and emergent) to avoid appearance shortcuts; 3) Organization of units to handle variable-length patterns beyond fixed patch boundaries.

paper.title: Faithful in Steps: Improving Generalization and Citation in RAG via Query Decomposition
paper.summary: Retrieval-augment generation is a prevalent strategy to mitigate hallucinations of LLMs. The attributable RAG (RAGQ) generates quotes for its answers. The quotes indicate which input contexts support the RAG to derive the answers, enhancing the answer's verifiability and trustworthiness. However, existing RAGQs exhibit significant degradation when dealing with questions that require multi-hop reasoning and multi-modal understanding, suffering from over-citation, implicit entity identification failure, and poor generalization. In this paper, we propose a novel RAGQ framework, namely QDRAG. QDRAG breaks down the input question into atomic subquestions to identify the implicit entities. Then, the reranker prunes context distractors to eliminate the downstream over-citation. To facilitate query decomposition, we propose two zero-shot approaches: QD-C and QD-R, which guide the QD MLLM to decompose the question based on context knowledge and retrieval rewards, respectively. One interesting finding is that finetuning on the QD task shows better generalizability compared to directly finetuning on the downstream RAGQ task. Experiments on four multi-modal QA benchmarks demonstrate QDRAG's efficacy in grounding answers and generating faithful citations. The framework significantly outperforms all the baselines on both in-domain and out-of-domain tests, even surpassing Gemini-Pro.

analysis.problem_statement: Existing attributable Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems suffer from over-citation, implicit entity identification failures, and poor generalization when handling multi-hop reasoning and multi-modal questions.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Hallucination mitigation and verifiability in multi-modal RAG systems, specifically addressing the gap between retrieval accuracy and faithful citation generation in complex reasoning tasks.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the critical need for trustworthy and verifiable AI outputs by improving the faithfulness of citations in multi-modal RAG systems. By introducing a query decomposition framework (QDRAG), it enhances the model's ability to identify implicit entities and prune distractors, resulting in more accurate and grounded answers. The finding that fine-tuning on query decomposition generalizes better than direct task fine-tuning offers a strategic insight for improving LLM robustness in complex reasoning scenarios.

paper.title: The Illusion of Diversity: Aligning LLM Exploration via Effective Entropy
paper.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has shifted the alignment paradigm of large language models from subjective preference to objective correctness, yet a fundamental disconnect persists between exploration diversity and reasoning validity. Existing strategies predominantly rely on "blind" entropy metrics, e.g., token-level or global sequence-level entropy, which structurally fail to distinguish between effective reasoning and potential hallucinations. This misalignment creates an illusion of diversity, where high entropy tends to signal chaotic degeneration rather than valuable exploration. To bridge this gap, we introduce Effective Entropy, a validity-aware entropy concept that quantifies diversity exclusively within the valid subspace and systematically filters out the noise of incorrect trajectories. Built on this concept, we instantiate VEPO, a simple Validity-aware Entropy Policy Optimization method that directly incorporates effective entropy into RLVR training. VEPO induces an adaptive attraction dynamic that drives up the probability of under-explored valid trajectories, a mechanism that matches the practical regime of large-scale autoregressive models where sequence probabilities remain extremely small. Experiments on six mathematical reasoning benchmarks with 1.5B and 7B DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen models show consistent aggregate accuracy gains over GRPO and competitive repeated-sampling success. A direct evaluation with matched correct counts finds more distinct strategies on commonly solved MATH500 problems, supported by paired statistical tests and three-seed training comparisons.

analysis.problem_statement: Standard entropy metrics in RLVR fail to distinguish between valid reasoning diversity and hallucinatory noise, creating an 'illusion of diversity' that hinders effective exploration in LLM alignment.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Exploration efficiency and validity alignment in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR).
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses a critical flaw in current LLM alignment where high entropy is incorrectly interpreted as valuable exploration, often masking chaotic degeneration. By introducing 'Effective Entropy' to quantify diversity only within the valid subspace, the method enables more targeted policy optimization. This is significant for advancing objective correctness in reasoning models by ensuring that exploration efforts are directed toward valid, under-explored trajectories rather than noise.

key_metrics.metric_value: Consistent aggregate accuracy gains; more distinct strategies on commonly solved problems.

paper.title: Loyalty Capture: Reporting Relationships and Structural Sycophancy in Frontier AI Models
paper.summary: We show that AI models exhibit loyalty capture, a form of structural sycophancy in which reporting relationships influence models' recommendations to serve the personal interests of their supervisors, without any explicit instruction, user feedback, or adversarial prompting. Specifically, models reporting to a CEO are significantly more likely to recommend cutting investment spending when the CEO's bonus depends on raising current period earnings. This effect is predictably absent from a metric-irrelevant placebo. The behavior appears consistent with loyalty-based motivated reasoning: models identify the bonus target, calculate how their recommendation helps achieve the target, and dismiss considerations of long-term value, often presenting their recommendations without treating the incentive as a conflict of interest. Prompt-based interventions help whereas generic conflict disclosures or stakeholder bargaining fail to eliminate it. Taken together, our findings indicate that AI models deployed within reporting relationships can act in favor of their supervisor's incentives at the expense of the organizations they are meant to serve.

paper.title: Read and Ignore: What Self-Directed LLM Agents Do in Public Service Scenarios
paper.summary: Underspecified instructions leave LLM agents to decide what to do. In public services, staff write these instructions, but the agent's decisions affect residents, patients, and students. We build four expert-validated public-service scenarios with records and decision levers that can be checked in the files, collect $2{,}400$ trajectories from ten LLMs under four prompt conditions, and compare them with $1{,}000$ runs in a context-free sandbox. Agents read the records in $96.9\%$ of open-ended runs and produce an artifact or a self-chosen task in $18.7\%$; with an explicit task, $86.0\%$ produce. Domain context does not change how many runs produce ($18.7\%$ vs.\ $16.0\%$), and the production ranking of the models largely carries over (Spearman $0.79$), while the ranking by whether a model reads the records does not ($0.19$). Context cuts boundary-probing turns per run by $60\%$, and some artifacts contradict the records. We contribute a test that a public-service institution can run on its own records before procurement; its rule-based taxonomy needs no labeled data, and scenarios, code, and trajectories are released.

analysis.problem_statement: The paper investigates how self-directed LLM agents behave when given underspecified instructions in high-stakes public service scenarios, specifically analyzing their decision-making, record utilization, and adherence to domain constraints.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Trust and reliability of autonomous LLM agents in safety-critical, real-world administrative contexts where explicit task definitions are absent or ambiguous.
analysis.executive_summary: This study provides a rigorous empirical evaluation of LLM agent autonomy in public service settings, revealing that while agents frequently read available records, their propensity to generate actionable artifacts is low without explicit tasks. It demonstrates that domain context significantly reduces boundary-probing behaviors but does not substantially increase production rates, highlighting a critical gap between agent capability and reliable deployment in institutional workflows.

key_metrics.baseline: Context-free sandbox runs

paper.title: Bet Imaginatively, not Historically in Independent-Data Sequential Testing
paper.summary: Sequential testing avoids some of the many controversies and drawbacks related to traditional batch testing with p-values. In particular, the testing by betting paradigm has developed rapidly in recent years; it frames the level of evidence against the null as the wealth of a player in a betting game. Naturally, how much a player should bet is a key consideration, and should reflect their confidence in what they know about the next observed data point. Much current work uses standard betting strategies developed for adversarial problems. In the stochastic setting, where the observed data is independent and stationary, these approaches may be suboptimal. We propose a simple betting strategy, follow the leave-one-out e-power (FLOE), that exploits the i.i.d. nature of a data stream to estimate the e-power of our current test on the underlying distribution. We average not over the historical evidence collected so far, as generic online learning-based methods do, but instead over the equally-likely possible data sequences we might have seen based on shuffling the data. With an additional principled regularization technique, this simple drop-in method yields substantial improvements in testing performance on a variety of kernel two-sample and independence testing problems.

analysis.problem_statement: Standard sequential testing strategies derived from adversarial online learning are suboptimal for independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) data streams because they do not fully exploit the stochastic nature of the data to optimize betting amounts.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Inefficiency in statistical hypothesis testing for i.i.d. data due to reliance on adversarial worst-case betting strategies rather than distribution-aware optimization.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses a gap in sequential statistical inference by proposing a betting strategy tailored for i.i.d. data, which is common in many AI and data science applications. By leveraging the independence of data points to estimate e-power more accurately, the method improves the speed and power of hypothesis tests compared to generic online learning approaches.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Testing performance (power/efficiency) in kernel two-sample and independence testing
key_metrics.metric_value: Substantial improvements (specific numerical values not provided in summary)
key_metrics.baseline: Standard betting strategies developed for adversarial problems (generic online learning-based methods)

technical_breakdown.method: Follow the Leave-One-Out e-Power (FLOE) strategy, which estimates the e-power of the current test by averaging over equally likely possible data sequences generated by shuffling the observed data, rather than averaging over historical evidence.
technical_breakdown.architecture: A drop-in replacement for the betting strategy component within the testing-by-betting framework, incorporating a principled regularization technique.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Uses leave-one-out estimation on shuffled data sequences to exploit i.i.d. properties; applies regularization to stabilize the betting strategy.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Implies additional computational overhead for shuffling and leave-one-out estimation compared to simple historical averaging, but remains a drop-in method for existing sequential testing frameworks.

paper.title: Reading the Unreadable: Text-Aware Image Super-Resolution Needs Reasoning
paper.summary: Text-aware image super-resolution (TAISR) aims to recover high-resolution images from low-resolution inputs while preserving textual content. Existing methods treat this as a visual restoration problem, yet severely degraded text often cannot be read from local visual evidence alone. Humans instead read it by reasoning over image context, logical patterns, and prior knowledge. This raises a fundamental question: Does TAISR need reasoning? To answer this, we introduce two diagnostic tools. The first, ReasonText, is a human-curated benchmark that separates reasoning-required text from locally recoverable text. The second, Ground-Truth Text-Crop Accuracy (GTTCA), is a recognition-based metric that measures text restoration quality without text detection errors. Evaluating twelve recent super-resolution (SR) models, we find a consistent and substantial performance drop on reasoning-required text, revealing a systematic blind spot. Two observations point to a remedy. One is that text-conditioned SR models restore text substantially better when given ground-truth text. The other is that multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can read degraded text in low-resolution images through reasoning. We therefore propose Reasoning Transfer via Captioning (RTC), a training-free plug-in that uses an external MLLM to infer the degraded text and feeds the resulting caption to a text-conditioned SR model. RTC consistently improves all six text-conditioned SR models we evaluate, especially on reasoning-required text. Surprisingly, a real-world SR model with RTC can even outperform the TAISR model with RTC, suggesting that reasoning should be a core design axis for future TAISR.

analysis.problem_statement: Existing text-aware image super-resolution (TAISR) methods fail to recover severely degraded text that cannot be reconstructed from local visual evidence alone, as they lack the reasoning capabilities humans use to infer content from context and prior knowledge.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: The lack of semantic reasoning and contextual inference in visual restoration models, specifically the inability to resolve ambiguous or corrupted textual information without external logical deduction.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper identifies a systematic blind spot in current super-resolution models where text recovery fails when local visual cues are insufficient, demonstrating that reasoning is a critical missing component. By introducing a training-free plug-in that leverages Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to infer text before restoration, it bridges the gap between visual restoration and semantic understanding. The findings suggest that integrating reasoning capabilities should become a core design axis for future high-fidelity image restoration tasks.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Ground-Truth Text-Crop Accuracy (GTTCA) on reasoning-required text
key_metrics.baseline: Twelve recent super-resolution models and text-conditioned SR models without reasoning

technical_breakdown.method: Reasoning Transfer via Captioning (RTC), a training-free plug-in that uses an external MLLM to infer degraded text from low-resolution images and feeds the resulting caption to a text-conditioned SR model.
technical_breakdown.architecture: A two-stage pipeline comprising an external MLLM for text inference/captioning and a downstream text-conditioned Super-Resolution model for image restoration.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Utilizes human-curated benchmark (ReasonText) to separate reasoning-required from locally recoverable text; employs GTTCA metric to measure restoration quality independent of detection errors; applies RTC to six text-conditioned SR models.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Training-free for the SR component; computational cost is dominated by the inference of the external MLLM, which adds latency but requires no retraining of the base SR models.

paper.title: Escaping the Curse of Dimensionality in One-Step Flow-Based Generative Models
paper.summary: Flow and diffusion-based generative models achieve state-of-the-art quality, but require multiple forward passes at inference time, making them computationally costly. Consistency models overcome this by learning a flow map directly, enabling few-step generation and dramatically reducing the computation needed at test time. However, formal statistical guarantees for such one-step generators are scarce. Existing results either suffer from the curse of dimensionality or rely on impractical loss functions. We investigate whether one-step flow-based models can escape the curse of dimensionality under the assumption that the data distribution is generated by a low-dimensional surface perturbed with Gaussian noise. In this setup, we derive approximation and generalization error bounds for the flow map estimate that circumvent the curse of dimensionality. Our findings provide the first principled explanation for practical success of one-step flow-based generative models.

analysis.problem_statement: The paper addresses the lack of formal statistical guarantees for one-step flow-based generative models, specifically investigating whether they can avoid the curse of dimensionality when the data lies on a low-dimensional manifold.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Computational inference cost and lack of theoretical convergence guarantees for few-step generative models.
analysis.executive_summary: This work provides the first principled theoretical explanation for the practical success of one-step flow-based models by deriving error bounds that do not scale exponentially with dimension. It resolves a key gap in the statistical theory of consistency models, showing that under low-dimensional manifold assumptions, these models can generalize effectively without the curse of dimensionality.

key_metrics.baseline: Existing results that suffer from the curse of dimensionality or rely on impractical loss functions.

technical_breakdown.method: The authors analyze one-step flow-based models under the assumption that the data distribution is generated by a low-dimensional surface perturbed with Gaussian noise. They derive approximation and generalization error bounds for the flow map estimate that circumvent the curse of dimensionality.

technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Statistical analysis of flow map estimation; assumption of low-dimensional surface plus Gaussian noise; derivation of error bounds independent of ambient dimension.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Theoretical analysis; no specific computational complexity or training time metrics provided in the summary.

paper.title: Verifier Choice is a Benchmark Design Variable: Auditing Structural Counting Evaluation in Text-to-Image Models
paper.summary: Automatic evaluation is now central to text-to-image benchmarking, but the verifier that converts generated images into scores is often treated as an implementation detail. We argue that this is unsafe: an automatic benchmark score is a property of the image generator, prompt distribution, verifier, verifier-use protocol, and scoring rule, not of the generator alone. We study this issue in structural counting, a controlled setting where human-visible counts can be audited. We construct a verifier-centric audit suite over seven counting objects: cell phones, chairs, and traffic lights for object counting, and clover leaflets, dresser drawer fronts, power-strip sockets, and turbine blades for substructure counting. Across 6,240 generated images from Qwen-Image-2512 and FLUX.2-dev, we compare open MLLM verifiers under count-only, reject-aware, zero-shot and few-shot protocols, plus TIFA-like target queries, a detector baseline, and frontier closed-model checks on two hard objects. On a balanced 2,280-image evaluation split, aggregate score matching can coexist with image-level disagreement, and verifier-use protocols and generator distributions change the measured reliability. Every verifier-protocol configuration also shrinks the human score difference between the two generators, by 7.5-25.0 pp, and with a third generator, Z-Image, all four tested protocols reverse the human ordering of Z-Image and FLUX.2-dev on our fixed prompt suite. GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.7 checks do not remove the failure modes: GPT-5.5 still has only 59.92% clover valid-count fidelity, while Claude Opus 4.7 has lower same-slice agreement ($κ=0.432$). We propose reporting automatic benchmark scores with a factorized verifier reliability profile: aggregate score gap, image-level agreement, generator-comparison distortion, valid-image count fidelity, rejection behavior, output compliance, and directional bias.

paper.title: Overcoming the Resolution Limit: Significance-Aware Regularization for Intersectional Fairness
paper.summary: Intersectional fairness requires evaluating models across fine-grained subgroups. However, as group definitions become more granular, the sample size per subgroup shrinks, causing fairness estimates to become increasingly unstable. Existing in-processing methods are certainty-blind: they penalize observed disparities without distinguishing statistically certified unfairness from sampling noise. This leads to fairness overfitting, where models sacrifice utility to "fix" spurious disparities in sparse regimes. To address this, we introduce the significant-excess metric family, a continuous, uncertainty-aware fairness score that measures only the portion of a subgroup's disparity exceeding what sampling variation can explain at a specific confidence level. Building on this metric, we propose SAFER (Significance-Aware Fairness Regularizer), a differentiable in-processing method that gates fairness penalties using a soft-count likelihood-ratio evidence statistic. SAFER satisfies a provable safety property: when every subgroup disparity lies well below the gate threshold, the unconstrained optimum is nearly stationary for SAFER. At that optimum, the back-propagated contribution of its significance-gated component is exponentially small, and the additional fairness contribution comes from a small ungated term with a fixed weight. Mechanism ablations across three benchmark datasets and purpose-built stress variants show that removing any component of SAFER (threshold smoothing, the significance gate, or a dense-tail term) produces the failure the theory predicts on at least one stress variant. In sparse intersectional settings, SAFER achieves a better fairness-utility Pareto frontier than the baseline methods, and it preserves utility when certified unfairness is absent.

analysis.problem_statement: Existing in-processing fairness methods suffer from 'fairness overfitting' in sparse intersectional subgroups by penalizing sampling noise as if it were certified unfairness, thereby unnecessarily sacrificing model utility.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Statistical instability and sample size limitations in fine-grained subgroup evaluation for intersectional fairness.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the critical trade-off between fairness and utility in intersectional settings where subgroup sample sizes are too small for stable statistical estimation. By introducing a significance-aware regularization that distinguishes between true disparity and sampling noise, it prevents models from over-correcting spurious disparities. This is vital for deploying fair AI systems in real-world scenarios where demographic intersections are often sparse.

key_metrics.baseline: Existing certainty-blind in-processing methods

paper.title: Learning Motion-Appearance Coupling Priors for Solving Video Inverse Problems
paper.summary: Reconstructing video from degraded measurements requires priors that capture both frame appearance and temporal dynamics. Many recent approaches combine pretrained image diffusion priors with motion guidance, sidestepping the costs of training large video models. Temporal consistency is often enforced via photometric losses or warping-based constraints, which implicitly assume that motion explains frame-to-frame or latent-to-latent changes up to small deviations, an assumption that fails under occlusions, lighting changes, and non-rigid deformation. In this paper, we propose to learn the coupling between motion and frame appearance as a generative prior. We learn the distribution of motion-induced appearance residuals with a conditional diffusion model and use it to regularize reconstruction in video inverse problems. Our motion-appearance prior acts as a plug-in regularizer for diffusion-based video reconstruction, preserving the benefits of image diffusion models while remaining compatible with existing appearance regularization techniques. Experiments on dynamic video inverse problems show that reconstruction with a learnt motion-appearance coupling prior outperforms photometric-consistency and noise-warping baselines, and that the approach also transfers to cardiac MRI reconstruction.

analysis.problem_statement: Reconstructing high-quality video from degraded measurements is hindered by the failure of standard temporal consistency constraints (like photometric loss) to handle occlusions, lighting changes, and non-rigid deformations.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: The lack of a robust generative prior that explicitly models the complex, non-rigid coupling between motion and appearance residuals in video reconstruction, which existing warping-based methods fail to capture.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses a critical limitation in video inverse problems where standard motion compensation fails under realistic conditions like occlusion and lighting shifts. By learning a conditional diffusion prior for motion-induced appearance residuals, it provides a plug-in regularizer that enhances reconstruction quality without requiring the training of massive video-specific models. This approach bridges the gap between efficient image diffusion priors and the temporal consistency required for dynamic video tasks, including medical imaging applications like cardiac MRI.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Reconstruction quality in dynamic video inverse problems
key_metrics.baseline: Photometric-consistency and noise-warping baselines

technical_breakdown.method: The method learns the distribution of motion-induced appearance residuals using a conditional diffusion model. This learned prior acts as a regularizer during the reconstruction process, correcting for deviations that simple warping cannot explain.
technical_breakdown.architecture: A conditional diffusion model trained on motion-appearance coupling data, integrated as a plug-in regularizer into existing diffusion-based video reconstruction frameworks.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Uses a conditional diffusion model to model the residuals between warped frames and actual frames. It is compatible with existing appearance regularization techniques and image diffusion priors.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Adds the computational cost of training and sampling a conditional diffusion model for residuals, but avoids the high cost of training large end-to-end video models.

paper.title: Is the Importance Ratio Necessary for Stable Reinforcement Learning in LLMs?
paper.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become central to post-training large language models (LLMs). However, popular RL methods like GRPO incur non-negligible overhead by computing both old-policy and current-policy likelihoods to form importance sampling ratios. In this work, we propose Likelihood-Gated Policy Optimization (LGPO), which enforces a soft trust region constraint via likelihood-based gating, eliminating the need to compute old-policy likelihoods. Empirically, we show that removing the importance sampling correction term does not harm training stability, whereas removing the trust region mechanism can lead to collapse. Moreover, ratio-based clipping can fail in fully on-policy training: the importance ratio stays at 1, so the ratio-based trust region constraint never activates. Under standard training settings where GRPO is stable, LGPO achieves comparable training stability and peak performance while reducing training time by ~18% on average relative to a standard implementation that recomputes old-policy likelihoods. In fully on-policy training, where GRPO fails, LGPO remains stable, enabling more efficient and robust LLM RL post-training across training regimes.

analysis.problem_statement: The paper addresses the computational overhead and instability issues associated with computing importance sampling ratios in reinforcement learning algorithms like GRPO for large language models.

paper.title: Track4D: Representing Dense 3D Tracking for Video Diffusion Models
paper.summary: We study how to repurpose video diffusion models (VDMs), pretrained on millions of videos, for dense 3D point tracking, where training data is scarce. Doing so is non-trivial, as it requires representing 3D tracks as video-like signals that may lie outside the natural-video distribution on which the VDM was trained. We thus systematically assess the effectiveness of two such video representations. The first, Residual 3D Tracking Video (RTV), encodes per-pixel 3D offsets relative to a query frame and allows recovery of 3D trajectories directly from the generated video. The second, Normalized Coordinate Map Video (NCMV), labels each pixel with a canonical coordinate invariant through time. This is closer to a natural video and easier for the VDM to learn, but requires additional post-processing with an off-the-shelf 2D tracker to recover 3D tracks. RTV tracks more accurately, while NCMV shows that a VDM can generate dense correspondence as a video. We instantiate both representations with LoRA adaptation of a frozen Wan backbone, conditioned on point maps from an off-the-shelf 3D reconstructor as a geometric scaffold. Trained with a single dynamic 3D tracking dataset, Track4D achieves competitive zero-shot tracking on four real and synthetic benchmarks. A regression readout that bypasses the video VAE and uses additional training data brings further improvement, demonstrating the potential of this direction for dense 3D tracking. We hope our analysis will inspire future work that leverages VDM priors for dense 3D tracking and 4D reconstruction. Project page: https://nirvanalan.github.io/projects/track4d

analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the challenge of leveraging large-scale video diffusion models for 3D tracking by systematically evaluating two video-like representations of 3D tracks. It demonstrates that VDMs can be adapted via LoRA to generate dense 3D correspondences, bridging the gap between 2D video generation and 4D reconstruction tasks.

paper.title: Measuring Robustness and Efficiency in a Connectome-Constrained Fly Visual System Model: Linking an Adversarial and a Perceptual Illusion
paper.summary: Biological visual systems compute reliably under tight metabolic and wiring constraints, whereas artificial vision systems consume far more energy and can be sensitive to adversarial perturbations. Whether networks with brain-like wiring are more robust at lower computational cost is unclear. We address this by benchmarking a task-optimized, continuous-time recurrent neural network of the fly visual system constrained by its synaptic connectome (FlyNet) against artificial neural networks. We compare it against CNNs, RAFT, and continuous-time recurrent neural networks without detailed connectome constraints (sCTRNN, CTRNN) on a collision-detection task within a differentiable 3D rendering pipeline. FlyNet is adversarially vulnerable but, relative to its compute, more robust to common video corruptions than RAFT, while using up to five orders of magnitude fewer FLOPs. The CTRNNs remain more robust than FlyNet across almost all tested perturbations, suggesting that connectome constraints benefit efficiency, through their low edge count, over robustness. Recurrence improves robustness to white-box attacks in RAFT and temporal context improves robustness to common corruptions. FlyNet's position and velocity representations degrade under adversarial textures but recover under counterfactual textures that restore correct classification while staying equally far from training, ruling out unfamiliar textures as the cause of failure. The reverse-phi illusion similarly disrupts these representations and inverts the same low-level motion statistic as the adversarial textures. Optimizing this input statistic alone, without access to the network, suffices to induce classification failure, attributing both perturbations to the same circuit vulnerability. Connectome-constrained models can thus surface adversarial failure mechanisms as testable hypotheses about biological perceptual vulnerabilities.

analysis.executive_summary: This study bridges the gap between biological vision and artificial intelligence by demonstrating that connectome-constrained models (FlyNet) achieve significant computational efficiency (up to 5 orders of magnitude fewer FLOPs) compared to standard artificial networks. It reveals that while these constraints favor efficiency over raw robustness, they expose specific circuit vulnerabilities that align with biological perceptual illusions, offering a new framework for understanding adversarial failures.

paper.title: OpticalRAG: Pixel-Space Compression for Token-Efficient Retrieval-Augmented Generation
paper.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is bottlenecked by the token budget of large language models: feeding long documents into the context window is expensive, while aggressive textual compression discards fine-grained information that is irreversibly lost in a one-dimensional token sequence. We argue that this bottleneck is not fundamental to information density but to the choice of compression \emph{modality}. Modern visual encoders can pack the contents of a rendered text page into roughly a hundred visual tokens with little semantic loss, opening a new compression-fidelity tradeoff that purely textual methods cannot reach. We present \textbf{OpticalRAG}, a framework that renders documents as page images, encodes them with a frozen vision encoder, and distills the retrieved visual tokens into as few as $16$ injected tokens before passing them to the LLM. Two ingredients make this work without expensive cross-modal training: (i) \emph{Encoder-Bridged Retrieval}, which projects text-query states into the visual feature space of the frozen encoder, through a projection shared with the compressor, to retrieve visual tokens from a text query, with no contrastive training; and (ii) \emph{Query-Driven Distillation}, a lightweight cross-attention compressor that condenses the retrieved visual tokens into a small set of query-conditioned prefix tokens. On LongBench-v2, BAMBOO, and LooGLE-v2, OpticalRAG achieves the best compression-aware accuracy (CAP) on all three benchmarks while injecting only $16$ tokens, and improves the closed-book Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct backbone by $5.17$ points on LongBench-v2. Code is available at https://github.com/brighterr/OpticalRAG.

analysis.executive_summary: This paper introduces a modality shift for RAG compression, utilizing visual encoders to pack document content into a small number of visual tokens with higher semantic fidelity than textual methods. By distilling these visual tokens into a minimal set of injected tokens, it enables efficient retrieval without expensive cross-modal training, addressing the tradeoff between compression ratio and information retention.

paper.title: Alignment De-Identifies Without Aligning: A Congruence-Invariant Relational Gap in Cross-Subject Neural Representations
paper.summary: In brain-computer interfaces, inter-subject variability remains a major challenge that limits decoding performance across users. Subject-wise alignment is widely used to improve cross-subject transfer of neural decoders, yet it is typically evaluated only through decoding accuracy, which cannot determine whether aligned representations share greater task-related structure. We therefore distinguish two questions that accuracy conflates: whether alignment removes subject-specific information and whether it makes the relational organization of task conditions more similar across individuals. Using three motor imagery-EEG cohorts, trials are represented as covariance matrices and aligned by recentering each subject's mean covariance to a common reference. Subject-specific information is quantified with a subject-identification probe, whereas relational structure is assessed using representational dissimilarity matrices (RDMs) computed from condition means with the affine-invariant Riemannian distance. We show that recentering leaves this distance, and therefore the resulting RDMs, unchanged. Consistent with this result, recentering reduces subject identification accuracy from 0.96 to chance level across all cohorts, while altering RDMs only at numerical precision. Cross-subject agreement in relational structure is significantly above zero but below the estimator's lower noise ceiling. Introducing an explicit similarity regularizer during training also fails to increase held-out agreement: the apparent reduction in between-subject differences is explained by a decline in the reliability ceiling rather than improved alignment. These findings show that eliminating subject identity is not equivalent to aligning relational geometry. More broadly, alignment claims must be interpreted relative to the invariances of both the distance and the statistic used to evaluate them.

analysis.executive_summary: This work demonstrates that standard covariance recentering in EEG-based BCIs is congruence-invariant, meaning it eliminates subject identity but leaves the Riemannian geometry of task conditions unchanged. It challenges the prevailing assumption that improved cross-subject decoding accuracy stems from better alignment of task representations, highlighting a critical gap in how alignment methods are evaluated and interpreted in neuro-AI.

paper.title: A General Concept-based Decomposition for Vision-Language Embeddings
paper.summary: Vision-Language Models are designed to capture the compositional structure of the world through multi-modal alignment; however, it remains unclear whether their representations truly align with the way a human would naturally describe the same visual input. Prior works attempt to decompose visual embeddings into their concept-level contributions, but their instance-level optimization is inherently local and does not capture the model's global semantic structure, which is essential for compositional generalization across different inputs, tasks, and domains. We introduce GRACE, a method that learns this concept-based structure at the feature space level, producing semantic and general concept decompositions. To achieve this, we propose a novel training objective that preserves the geometric relations of different samples in the concept space, enabling a better understanding of how concepts compose and relate to each other. We validate GRACE on several image and video benchmarks, showing that its concept decomposition is aligned with human perception and achieves faithful decompositions across different tasks and domains. With minimal overhead, GRACE makes existing Vision-Language Models more interpretable, while preserving most of their original performance.

paper.title: HyperSkill: Training-Free Omnimodal GRPO via Hypergraph-Indexed Skill-Library Evolution
paper.summary: Reinforcement learning sharpens LLM reasoning, but parameter updates are expensive, forgetful, and opaque; training-free libraries swap gradients for a textual store but still use trajectory-level, correlation-based admission and flat structure. To address both, we propose HyperSkill, a Training-Free Omnimodal GRPO framework that keeps the backbone frozen and replaces gradient updates with auditable edits to a Hypergraph-Indexed Skill-Library, where skills are advantage-bearing nodes and compositions are hyperedges. It has three components: training-time distillation admits counterfactually checked skills and learns a protocol skill from failures; gated hypergraph retrieval injects advantage-ranked skills where a per-dataset gate admits them; and an execution protocol makes the frozen backbone commit to an answer. On 11 text, vision-language, and omnimodal benchmarks, HyperSkill is best or tied on every dataset and beats the best baseline by 13.0 average F1 points while keeping the backbone frozen. Our software and data are publicly available at https://github.com/LHRLAB/HyperSkill.

analysis.executive_summary: HyperSkill offers a training-free alternative to gradient-based RL by evolving a hypergraph-indexed skill library, allowing frozen LLM backbones to improve reasoning without parameter updates. This approach reduces training costs and enhances auditability by replacing opaque weight changes with explicit, advantage-bearing textual skills and compositions.

paper.title: CineMME: From Dialogue Grounding to Narrative Reasoning in Multimodal Video Understanding
paper.summary: Narrative video understanding requires more than recognizing visible events: models must extract evidence from dialogue, bind it to speakers, and use it to infer narrative meaning. Existing video benchmarks evaluate aspects of this problem, including video question answering, audio-visual reasoning, and temporal grounding, but rarely test whether these abilities form a coherent dialogue-to-plot evidence chain within the same clips. We introduce \textbf{CineMME}, a human-verified benchmark designed to diagnose dialogue-grounded plot understanding, supported by approximately $1,600$ expert person-hours of annotation. CineMME contains $975$ curated short narrative video clips and two linked tracks: \textit{CineMME-Grounding}, with $13,554$ timestamped speech segments and $33,083$ speaker face boxes for temporal dialogue localization, transcription, and active-speaker grounding; and \textit{CineMME-Reasoning}, with $1,600$ multiple-choice and $316$ open-ended questions spanning perception, audio, narrative, social, and scene-presentation understanding. Our main evaluation compares $20$ MLLMs on reasoning and $9$ omni-modal models on grounding. The results reveal a pronounced who-what-when decoupling: Gemini-3 Pro localizes dialogue in time ($68.34\%$ tIoU) and transcribes it with a WER of $28.99\%$, yet achieves only $7.74\%$ vIoU for active-speaker grounding while achieving $67.66\%$ MCQ accuracy on questions with extractable answers. Modality ablations further show that vision is not uniformly beneficial: it improves performance on perception-heavy questions but can hurt dialogue-centric reasoning. CineMME provides a compact diagnostic testbed for evaluating how multimodal video models connect dialogue, speakers, visual evidence, and narrative meaning.

paper.title: MatrixSplat: Matrix-Parallel and Feature-Scalable 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering on GPUs
paper.summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has emerged as a mainstream representation for real-time novel view synthesis and 3D reconstruction. However, existing 3DGS rendering pipelines are poorly aligned with modern GPU architectures: depth-sorted alpha compositing introduces strong per-pixel sequential dependencies, limiting parallelism and resulting in scalar FMA-dominated execution that underutilizes high-throughput matrix units such as Tensor Cores. This mismatch becomes more severe for multimodal and semantically enriched 3DGS, where high-dimensional features must be accumulated from millions of Gaussians, leading to rapidly increasing computation and memory costs. We propose MatrixSplat, a matrix-parallel rendering framework for feature-scalable 3DGS on modern GPUs. We first identify the sequential dependency of alpha compositing as a key obstacle to efficient high-dimensional feature rendering, and adopt an order-independent weighted accumulation formulation that transforms feature rendering into matrix-oriented computation. Our framework features three key designs: (i) a tile-based splatting pipeline that maps feature accumulation to warp-level matrix-multiply-accumulate execution on Tensor Cores; (ii) a warp-granularity Gaussian packing strategy that mitigates visibility irregularity and improves feature reuse; and (iii) a lazy channel-batched feature-fetching pipeline that reduces shared-memory pressure, maintains high warp occupancy, and overlaps memory access with matrix execution for high-dimensional features. On Mip-NeRF 360, LERF, and 3D-OVS, MatrixSplat achieves up to 3.8$\times$ speedup over 3DGS and 2$\times$ over TC-GS while maintaining rendering quality and semantic accuracy, and further reduces render-kernel time by up to 36.7$\times$ for high-dimensional features. Integrated into existing fast renderers, it provides an additional 1.69-2.84$\times$ speedup.

analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the critical mismatch between 3DGS rendering algorithms and modern GPU architectures by transforming sequential alpha compositing into matrix-parallel operations. It enables efficient rendering of semantically enriched, high-dimensional 3DGS models, which is essential for advancing multimodal 3D reconstruction and real-time novel view synthesis.

paper.title: Profile-Based Auditing of Domestic Violence Survey Selection Across South Asia
paper.summary: Domestic violence (DV) data in the Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) are collected through a specialized module whose household-level sampling and privacy requirements create a distinct observation process. We ask whether demographic, socioeconomic, and household characteristics form reproducible population profiles and whether these profiles contain information about selection into the DV module across South Asia. Using DHS Individual Recode data for 796,374 women aged 15-49 across Afghanistan, India, Myanmar, Nepal, and Pakistan, we harmonize 61 numeric and 8 categorical features, reduce the profile space with PCA, and identify six interpretable profiles. We then evaluate 22 machine-learning models under primary-sampling-unit-aware holdout validation. The best model, HistGradientBoosting, achieves ROC-AUC 0.9167 and PR-AUC 0.9612, versus 0.8475 and 0.9203 for a design-only baseline. Adding woman-level characteristics yields the largest incremental gain, while explicit interaction terms add little out-of-sample performance. Country-specific analyses reveal substantial heterogeneity, and leave-one-country-out evaluation shows that transferability of the incremental profile signal is limited. These results demonstrate that interpretable ML can audit differential coverage in sensitive survey modules beyond the formal sampling design.

analysis.executive_summary: This work demonstrates that interpretable machine learning can effectively audit the integrity of sensitive survey data by identifying reproducible population profiles that correlate with module selection. By outperforming design-only baselines, it provides a robust framework for ensuring data representativeness in global health research, which is critical for the reliability of AI models trained on such datasets.

paper.title: Prototypes of the Mind: A Unified Framework for Probing the Visual Brain
paper.summary: Deep learning has driven substantial progress in modeling fMRI responses, yet most existing approaches are optimized for a single objective---such as neural encoding, stimulus decoding, or post hoc interpretation---making it difficult to obtain a coherent account of neural representations. We introduce a unified framework that connects vision foundation models to brain activity while supporting neural analysis from multiple complementary perspectives. Our approach replaces black-box features with a sparse, interpretable representation composed of visual prototypes, and links these prototypes to voxel responses through a linear readout. This design makes the model transparent at both levels: prototype activations expose the visual concepts present in the stimulus, while the learned linear weights characterize each voxel's selectivity. Using this interface, we identify which visual concepts drive neural responses and where they appear in the image, reveal cortical organization through voxel tuning in prototype space, and perform controlled stimulus synthesis to probe cortical selectivity through targeted interventions. Together, these results establish prototype-based representations as a unified and interpretable foundation for studying visual representations in the human brain.

analysis.problem_statement: Existing deep learning approaches for modeling fMRI responses are typically optimized for single objectives (encoding, decoding, or interpretation), preventing a coherent and unified account of neural representations.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Lack of interpretability and unified representation in neuro-visual modeling, where black-box features obscure the link between visual concepts and specific neural selectivity.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper introduces a unified framework that bridges vision foundation models and brain activity by replacing opaque features with sparse, interpretable visual prototypes. It enables simultaneous analysis of neural encoding, decoding, and interpretation, providing a transparent view of how visual concepts map to voxel-level cortical selectivity.
