key_metrics.baseline: Existing single-objective approaches (neural encoding, stimulus decoding, or post hoc interpretation)

technical_breakdown.method: The framework connects vision foundation models to brain activity using a sparse, interpretable representation of visual prototypes linked to voxel responses via a linear readout.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Vision foundation models generating visual prototypes, followed by a linear readout layer mapping prototype activations to voxel responses.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Uses sparse prototype activations to expose visual concepts and learned linear weights to characterize voxel selectivity; supports controlled stimulus synthesis for targeted interventions.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Not specified in summary, but implies linear readout complexity on top of foundation model inference.

paper.title: SkinAdvisor: An AI-Driven Decision Framework for Skin Production Planning via Multi-Modal Transformer Sales Forecasting
paper.summary: Skins, cosmetic in-game items, are a primary revenue stream for modern online games, yet production decisions (which skins to make, when to release, how to price) remain driven by intuition and retrospective analytics. We present SkinAdvisor, an AI-driven decision framework for skin production planning, powered by SkinCast, a deployed multi-modal Transformer forecasting 180-day per-day sales trajectories for unreleased skins. SkinCast couples four encoders: a pretrained Informer for player-preference time series, a pretrained Player-Hero-Skin graph embedder for relational priors, and two lightweight Transformers for skin attributes and release context, fused through a shared backbone with a local-plus-global day-x positional encoding and decoded by an N-layer Informer in a single non-autoregressive pass. SkinAdvisor plugs these forecasts into a serving pipeline (Select -> Fill -> Infer -> Sales -> ROI -> Ranking) that ranks candidate skins by forecast-based ROI and supports multi-candidate comparison. The system has been in production for a full release cycle. Offline experiments show SkinCast reduces RMSE by ~20% over the strongest baseline (Informer) and ~60% over classical methods; stress tests on a 16-core CPU server confirm p99 latency under 8ms and peak throughput above 1100 rps. We report two deployment lessons: order-of-magnitude accuracy suffices for production decisions, and pretrained embeddings can leak temporal information, requiring season-based splitting to prevent.

analysis.problem_statement: The paper addresses the lack of data-driven, forward-looking decision-making in the production and pricing of cosmetic in-game items (skins), which currently relies on intuition and retrospective analytics.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: It addresses the bottleneck of integrating heterogeneous multi-modal data (time-series, graph, and attribute data) into low-latency, non-autoregressive forecasting systems for real-time business decision support.
analysis.executive_summary: This work demonstrates the practical application of multi-modal Transformer architectures in a high-stakes commercial gaming environment, bridging the gap between complex AI research and deployed production systems. It highlights that order-of-magnitude accuracy is sufficient for high-level production planning, challenging the need for extreme precision in all forecasting tasks. Additionally, it provides critical deployment insights regarding data leakage in pretrained embeddings, which is a significant concern for practitioners using pre-trained models in time-series contexts.

key_metrics.metric_value: ~20% reduction over strongest baseline; ~60% reduction over classical methods
key_metrics.baseline: Informer (strongest baseline) and classical methods

These are fused through a shared backbone with local-plus-global day-x positional encoding and decoded by an N-layer Informer in a single non-autoregressive pass.

technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Achieves p99 latency under 8ms and peak throughput above 1100 requests per second on a 16-core CPU server, indicating high efficiency and low computational overhead for inference.

paper.title: From Forecasting to World Modeling: Can Temporal Foundation Models Recover Causal Response?
paper.summary: A model that forecasts sales accurately can still mislead a retailer about how sales respond to a price change. We evaluate released tabular and time-series foundation models, as well as a foundation model pretrained specifically to estimate causal effects. We report three findings. First, forecast accuracy does not indicate the accuracy of the predicted effect of price, both on simulated data in which the true effect is known and on real retail sales records. Second, for the tabular foundation models, additional context improves forecasts but not the predicted effect of price. Third, instrumental variables, the standard remedy in econometrics, reduce this error only when supplied in a specific form and increase it for every model under confounding when supplied as raw instruments.

analysis.bottleneck_addressed: The gap between predictive performance (forecasting) and causal inference (counterfactual reasoning) in foundation models, where high accuracy in prediction does not guarantee correct understanding of causal mechanisms.
analysis.executive_summary: This work demonstrates that standard foundation models for time-series and tabular data fail to accurately estimate causal effects despite strong forecasting capabilities, highlighting a critical limitation for decision-support systems. It further reveals that simply adding context improves forecasts but not causal accuracy, and that standard econometric remedies like instrumental variables can paradoxically worsen causal estimates if not properly formatted, challenging common assumptions in applied AI and econometrics.

paper.title: Coarse-to-Fine 3D MRI Reconstruction via Resolution-Agnostic Neural Operators
paper.summary: Deep-learning-based 3D MRI reconstruction is limited in practice by the GPU memory and compute cost of full-volume training; 3D acquisitions are thus most often reconstructed by 2D models applied slice-by-slice and then stacked, which ignores through-plane (stacking-axis) structure. We reconstruct in full 3D and ask whether a model can be trained at low resolution (fast and memory-feasible) yet deployed at higher resolution. This coarse-to-fine strategy needs reliable cross-resolution performance, but standard networks are resolution-specific and degrade substantially when evaluated outside the training setting. We therefore use resolution-agnostic neural operators (NOs) and propose KIR-NO (k-space-to-Image Reconstruction Neural Operator), a discretization-agnostic framework for accelerated 3D MRI reconstruction. KIR-NO is trained with full backpropagation on low-resolution volumes and applied zero-shot to higher-resolution volumes at inference. Its core building block is a 3D neural operator based on discrete-continuous convolutions: convolutional filters are parameterized in a continuous basis and sampled at arbitrary voxel resolutions while preserving the local inductive bias of convolution. KIR-NO integrates these learned operators with physics-based consistency: a k-space neural-operator head first refines the undersampled Fourier measurements, and image-space neural-operator cascades then refine the reconstruction through interleaved data-consistency updates. Across 3D knee and brain MRI benchmarks, KIR-NO improves over classical and CNN baselines: it improves over a state-of-the-art 3D CNN by 2.2 dB PSNR at half resolution under 4x acceleration on SKM-TEA, with gains persisting at 8x and 16x. These results show that resolution-agnostic operators make coarse-to-fine 3D MRI reconstruction - cheap low-resolution training with high-resolution deployment - practical across anatomies.

analysis.problem_statement: Standard 3D MRI reconstruction models are resolution-specific and suffer from significant performance degradation when deployed at resolutions different from their training setting, limiting the feasibility of coarse-to-fine training strategies due to GPU memory constraints.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: GPU memory and compute costs associated with full-volume 3D training, and the lack of generalization across spatial resolutions in deep learning models.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the practical limitation of 3D MRI reconstruction by enabling models trained on low-resolution volumes to be deployed zero-shot at higher resolutions. By utilizing resolution-agnostic neural operators, it overcomes the memory bottlenecks of full-volume training while preserving through-plane structural information that slice-by-slice 2D models ignore.

key_metrics.baseline: State-of-the-art 3D CNN
key_metrics.improvement_percentage: Not explicitly quantified as a percentage in the summary; reported as 2.2 dB PSNR gain

technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Training is performed on low-resolution volumes to ensure memory feasibility and speed, while inference scales to higher resolutions without retraining, reducing overall computational cost compared to full-resolution 3D training.

paper.title: Aggregate Accuracy Hides Diagnosis-Specific Failure in Medical Vision-Language Models
paper.summary: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) are compared mainly by accuracy averaged across findings, a summary that can hide complete failure on a single diagnosis. We audit five open medical VLMs (MedGemma-4B, Lingshu-7B, HuatuoGPT-Vision-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and MedVLM-R1) on 6,048 ChestX-ray14 questions balanced by sex, age, finding, and label. On the 432 pneumothorax-positive X-rays, HuatuoGPT-Vision and Qwen2.5-VL detect zero cases while MedGemma and Lingshu detect 38% and 67% of the same images. The two failing models answer "no" to all 864 pneumothorax cases (balanced accuracy 0.500, chance), yet produce fluent, anatomically specific explanations that name the signs of a collapsed lung and then deny them, with no hedge or abstention. This failure is not an artifact of prompting, image resolution, label ambiguity, or model scale. It persists across four prompt formats, at native resolution, and on single-label cases. A within-model control shows the same forced prompt gives HuatuoGPT 79% recall on nodule but only 6% on pneumothorax. It survives a tenfold scale increase (Qwen2.5-VL-72B detects 4%) and replicates on SIIM-ACR, an independent dataset with radiologist-drawn masks, where the failing models detect 0 of 432 confirmed pneumothoraces, including 0 of the 144 largest lesions. Reading the models' logits and internal states shows this is not blindness. The two failing models are highly confident yet no better than chance and a linear probe recovers pneumothorax from their hidden representations even where recall is zero, so the finding is represented internally but suppressed at the output. Aggregate accuracy therefore cannot establish that a medical VLM can see a given finding, because a model that misses one can still describe it convincingly. Reporting per-finding recall and specificity on balanced cases is needed to tell the difference.

analysis.executive_summary: This study reveals that high aggregate accuracy in medical VLMs is misleading, as models can achieve chance-level performance on specific diagnoses (like pneumothorax) while generating fluent, anatomically correct but factually wrong explanations. It demonstrates that this failure is not due to lack of visual perception or prompting issues, but rather a suppression of internal representations at the output layer, highlighting the urgent need for per-finding recall and specificity metrics in medical AI validation.

paper.title: Binding Mode Matters: Hotspot-Aware Drug Discovery via Explorative Preferences
paper.summary: Discovering hit molecules requires not just high binding affinity, but also the identification of diverse binding modes, which are critical for experimental assays. Existing generative approaches have predominantly relied on optimizing a scalar docking score, obscuring the distinct contributions of key binding determinants. To this end, we introduce a paradigm shift by formulating target-based drug design as a multi-objective exploration task, where each objective explicitly corresponds to enhancing interactions with a specific hotspot. Here, we introduce BindMol, a novel generative framework driven by a customized multi-objective reinforcement learning algorithm. By incorporating explorative preferences during training, our approach efficiently uncovers molecules with diverse and desirable binding profiles. Empirical results demonstrate that BindMol facilitates the discovery of high-affinity compounds characterized by both structural novelty and diverse binding modes. Validated across target-based drug discovery and multi-property optimization tasks, our approach provides a versatile paradigm for goal-oriented drug discovery.

analysis.problem_statement: Existing generative drug discovery methods rely on scalar docking scores, which obscure the distinct contributions of specific binding hotspots and fail to ensure diverse binding modes necessary for experimental validation.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: The lack of interpretability and diversity in binding mode exploration due to the aggregation of complex molecular interactions into a single scalar optimization objective.
analysis.executive_summary: This work shifts target-based drug design from single-objective scalar optimization to a multi-objective exploration task, explicitly targeting individual binding hotspots. By using a customized multi-objective reinforcement learning framework, it enables the discovery of molecules with both high affinity and diverse, structurally novel binding profiles that are more likely to succeed in experimental assays.

key_metrics.baseline: Existing generative approaches optimizing scalar docking scores

technical_breakdown.architecture: BindMol generative framework incorporating explorative preferences during the training phase.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Customized multi-objective reinforcement learning algorithm that explicitly optimizes for interactions with specific hotspots rather than a global docking score.

paper.title: Speech Tokenizers are Vulnerable: Transferable Semantic Attack and Robust Tokenizer
paper.summary: Speech tokenizers serve as speech front ends, encoding input speech signals into representations for downstream models, such as automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems and large audio-language models (LALMs). In this paper, we find that speech tokenizers are fragile at the semantic level: small perturbations can disrupt their semantic encoding process and consequently cause severe degradation in downstream ASR and LALM performance. To study this vulnerability, we propose T-SemAttack, a transferable semantic attack based on a semantic encoder ensemble. By jointly drifting the representation spaces of multiple semantic encoders, T-SemAttack effectively disrupts the semantic content of speech while preserving perceptual quality, thereby inducing error features. We further analyze layer-wise representation drift and cross-model gradient alignment. Our findings show that perturbations can induce substantial shifts in deep semantic representations and that the input gradients of different surrogate encoders exhibit directional alignment. These observations suggest that shared adversarially sensitive directions in the input space may be a key factor underlying cross-model attack transferability. Building on these, we introduce ROSETok, a robust speech tokenizer that combines noisy training with robust semantic distillation to improve reconstruction fidelity and downstream SpeechLLM robustness. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets, 9 open-source and black-box ASR systems, and 4 LALMs demonstrate that T-SemAttack achieves strong transferable attack performance, while the proposed Robust Speech Tokenizer exhibits robustness under high-fidelity reconstruction and downstream tasks. Our code and demo are available at https://wxzyd123.github.io/t-semattack.

analysis.problem_statement: Speech tokenizers are vulnerable to small semantic-level perturbations that degrade downstream ASR and LALM performance without compromising perceptual audio quality.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Adversarial robustness and semantic integrity of speech front-end encoders in multimodal AI pipelines.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper exposes a critical security flaw in speech tokenizers, showing that they can be manipulated to induce severe errors in downstream models like ASR and LALMs while remaining imperceptible to human listeners. It provides both a transferable attack method (T-SemAttack) and a defensive solution (ROSETok), highlighting the need for robust semantic encoding in the era of large audio-language models.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Transferable attack success rate and downstream task robustness (WER/accuracy)
key_metrics.baseline: Standard speech tokenizers and vanilla ASR/LALM models

technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Joint drifting of multiple semantic encoder representation spaces; analysis of layer-wise representation drift and cross-model gradient alignment; noisy training and robust semantic distillation.

paper.title: Rethinking "RL Generalizes, SFT Memorizes": The Role of SFT Data
paper.summary: Large language models trained with Reinforcement Learning (RL) with verifiable rewards exhibit strong reasoning ability and broad generalization, whereas models trained with Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) are often viewed as more prone to memorization and limited transfer. This paper rethinks this distinction through the lens of SFT training data on widely used Qwen2.5 and Qwen3 series models. First, we study the role of data source and show that it is critical: a carefully mixed SFT dataset substantially outperforms data generated solely by a larger model. Second, we study the role of data scale and show that matching the number of correct rollouts between SFT and RL greatly improves SFT generalization, while matching the total rollout budget enables SFT to generalize as well as RL. Combining these two factors further enables SFT to generalize even better than RL. Third, by using LLM annotations to characterize the solution methods in training rollouts, we show that larger datasets cover more tail methods and that these tail methods provide generalizable reasoning signals. Finally, we support these empirical findings theoretically by analyzing the training dynamics of shallow transformers under both RL and SFT.

analysis.problem_statement: The paper challenges the prevailing assumption that Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) inherently leads to memorization and poor generalization compared to Reinforcement Learning (RL) by investigating how SFT data composition and scale influence this distinction.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Generalization gap between SFT and RL training paradigms in Large Language Models.
analysis.executive_summary: This work demonstrates that the perceived superiority of RL in generalization is largely attributable to data scale and diversity rather than the optimization objective itself. By matching the number of correct rollouts and total budget between SFT and RL, SFT can achieve comparable or even superior generalization performance. This suggests that careful curation of SFT data, particularly covering tail-end reasoning methods, is a viable alternative to complex RL pipelines for achieving robust reasoning capabilities.

key_metrics.metric_value: SFT generalizes as well as or better than RL when data scale and source are matched
key_metrics.baseline: RL with verifiable rewards on Qwen2.5 and Qwen3 series
key_metrics.improvement_percentage: Not quantified in summary; qualitative claim of 'as well as' or 'even better than'

technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Comparison of SFT datasets mixed from various sources vs. single-source generated data; matching correct rollout counts and total rollout budgets between SFT and RL; LLM-based annotation to characterize solution method diversity (tail methods).
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Requires large-scale rollout generation and training for both SFT and RL baselines; theoretical analysis involves shallow transformer dynamics.

paper.title: MuEdit: An efficient multi-task editing method towards inter-domain knowledge conflicts
paper.summary: Large language models (LLMs) require frequent knowledge updates across heterogeneous domains, but existing editing methods fail when applied sequentially to multi-task settings. We trace this collapse to inter-domain null-space misalignment: heterogeneous tasks induce distinct Jacobian geometries, causing their common null space to shrink dramatically and leaving insufficient admissible directions for conflict-free updates. We propose the Conflict Index to quantify this geometric interference, and introduce Mu-Edit, which mitigates multi-task conflicts via (1) conflict-aware ordering to minimize cumulative interference, and (2) dynamic low-rank approximation to expand the null space when ordering alone is insufficient. Experiments across five functional domains and three backbones show that Mu-Edit significantly outperforms existing baselines in multi-task editing performance while preserving general capabilities, and remains effective under incremental task arrival.

analysis.problem_statement: Existing knowledge editing methods for Large Language Models fail in multi-task settings due to inter-domain null-space misalignment, which shrinks the admissible parameter space for conflict-free updates.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Knowledge editing stability and scalability in multi-domain scenarios
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the critical limitation of sequential knowledge editing in LLMs, where heterogeneous tasks cause geometric conflicts that degrade model performance. By identifying and mitigating inter-domain null-space misalignment, MuEdit enables robust, conflict-free updates across multiple domains without sacrificing general capabilities.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Multi-task editing performance and preservation of general capabilities
key_metrics.baseline: Existing knowledge editing baselines

technical_breakdown.method: MuEdit utilizes a Conflict Index to quantify geometric interference between tasks and applies conflict-aware ordering to minimize cumulative interference, supplemented by dynamic low-rank approximation to expand the null space when necessary.
technical_breakdown.architecture: The method operates on the Jacobian geometry of the LLM, focusing on the common null space of heterogeneous tasks to ensure admissible update directions.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Key techniques include the calculation of a Conflict Index for geometric interference quantification, a conflict-aware task ordering algorithm, and a dynamic low-rank approximation mechanism to expand the null space.

paper.title: Imperfectly Imperfect: Evaluating Graded Cognitive Diversity in LLM Persona Simulations
paper.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used as synthetic participants in social, behavioural, and decision-making research, yet it remains unclear whether they can express graded cognitive diversity as assigned when engaging in simulated behaviour. We introduce a cognition-suite evaluation that tests whether simulated populations reproduce human variation in reasoning, self-reported traits, their associations, and downstream behaviour. Agents conditioned on synthetic or human-derived profiles of cognitive reflection, Need for Cognition, and Big Five personality answer the same suite as a cohort of 473 adults: two newly assembled tests, a Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT) and a Behavioural Reflection Test (BRT) whose decision scenarios measure reflection in behaviour, alongside an established CRT and the two trait questionnaires. Across seven full-battery simulation runs of four models, agents recover Need for Cognition and Big Five trait distributions on self-report questionnaires, but fall short on simulating diversity of cognitive task performance and downstream behaviours. In the four Claude Sonnet 4.6 runs, every agent scores full marks on both CRTs, whatever reflection level its persona was assigned. In the other three runs agents make intuitive-lure errors (the tempting wrong answers CRT items invite), but 49 to 85% score full marks, against under 10% in the human sample. Claude Sonnet 5 comes closest to people's item-by-item pattern of lures; the other two runs give fewer lures and vary less between items. In the BRT scenarios, every run over-produces 8 to 11 of 15 coded behaviours by at least 20 percentage points, and people's links between reflection and behaviour carry over only in part. Useful synthetic populations must preserve not only trait descriptors but the structured variation in reasoning, error type, and behaviour those descriptors are meant to organise.

analysis.executive_summary: This work demonstrates that while LLMs can mimic self-reported trait distributions, they critically fail to simulate the structured variation in actual cognitive task performance and behavior. The findings highlight a significant gap in using LLMs as synthetic participants in social and behavioral research, as they do not preserve the link between cognitive traits and reasoning errors.

paper.title: Towards Better Legal Reasoning LLMs: Signal Balancing and Reward Scheduling
paper.summary: In the legal domain, LLMs can improve reliability and interpretability by generating explicit reasoning traces. However, training LLMs to produce high-quality reasoning traces remains challenging. Existing supervised fine-tuning methods struggle when reasoning traces are significantly longer than final answers, as the learning signal for the answer becomes diluted. Meanwhile, reinforcement learning methods such as Group Relative Policy Optimization also have several limitations, including costly reward design, performance plateaus, and reward hacking. We therefore propose a two-stage training framework. In Stage I, JurisCoT-SFT employs a length-normalized dual objective to balance learning signals between reasoning traces and final answers. In Stage II, Lifecycle-Aware Backtrackable Policy Optimization dynamically evaluates and retires auxiliary reward signals based on their impact on final evaluation objectives, enabling efficient reward utilization. Our framework substantially improves legal reasoning performance on relevant tasks selected from multiple legal benchmarks, including ChJGBench, LawBench, and LegalBench. Experimental results demonstrate consistent improvements in both reasoning trace quality and final answer accuracy, while our models remain competitive with larger models.

paper.title: What Makes a VLA Reactive? A Study of Execution Strategies for Dynamic Manipulation
paper.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models predict chunks of future actions, and when objects move, those chunks go stale before they are executed. We study what makes a pretrained VLA reactive, using \pihalf{} on two dynamic simulation benchmarks and three real-robot tasks. We vary the prediction and execution horizons, compare synchronous and asynchronous inference, test methods that deliver actions sooner or keep successive chunks continuous, and adapt the policy with motion cues and latent-space reinforcement learning. The best prediction horizon is about one second, and the best execution horizon depends on the checkpoint. Short horizons help more with asynchronous execution, and methods that keep the trajectory continuous outperform those that only reduce latency. Adapting the policy repairs targeted failures, but on the conveyor task changing the execution horizon gained as much. Reactivity depends on the execution pipeline as much as on the policy, so both should be evaluated together.

It provides a systematic evaluation of how prediction and execution horizons, synchronous vs. asynchronous inference, and trajectory continuity methods impact performance in dynamic manipulation tasks.

paper.title: Prediction or Persistence? What Future-Prediction Scores Miss About World Models
paper.summary: Pretrained video world models are compared and chosen as components for robot learning largely by future-prediction scores. On its own, such a score cannot be read as evidence of prediction, because it mixes encoder quality, the near future's resemblance to the recent past, and the predictor's own contribution. We separate the three with a matched control. On 27,000 future-retrieval trials from household egocentric video, a model must pick the true continuation of a clip among eleven candidates from the same video (chance 0.091), ranked zero-shot by its own training criterion. Each model is paired with a persistence control, an identical copy whose predictor is never invoked, so the paired difference isolates the predictor. Score and contribution dissociate within the native-video V-JEPA family alone: the predictor adds +0.291 top-1 for V-JEPA 2.1 but +0.03 to +0.04 for V-JEPA 2 on the identical trials. Across five models the contribution ranges from +0.291 to negative, and it is negative only for the two action-conditioned models, which we evaluate outside their training regime. Persistence alone recovers the encoder ordering expected from pretraining, a sign that the probe tracks real signal. We suggest reporting each future-prediction score together with its persistence baseline. The gap between them, not the score, is what makes the number interpretable: a necessary check costing one forward pass. Establishing downstream usefulness is a separate matter, for a planning or control evaluation.

analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Evaluation methodology and interpretability of world model performance metrics.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper demonstrates that high future-prediction scores in robot learning world models are often driven by the encoder's ability to capture static features or the natural persistence of video sequences rather than the predictor's ability to model dynamics. By isolating the predictor's contribution using a matched persistence control, the study reveals significant dissociations between raw scores and actual predictive utility, particularly within the V-JEPA family. This work provides a necessary diagnostic tool to distinguish between models that genuinely predict the future and those that merely persist the past.

paper.title: CrowdMAPS: Crowdsourcing Multiple Actions per State for Real-World Imitation Learning
paper.summary: Real-world robot imitation learning is often limited by the cost of collecting physical demonstrations, which typically yield only one action label per visited state. We present CrowdMAPS, a web-based crowdsourcing paradigm for augmenting real-robot datasets with Multiple Actions per State (MAPS). After or during standard robot data collection, CrowdMAPS distributes visited robot states to remote annotators through a web-based 3D interface, where they specify alternative valid actions without requiring access to physical robot hardware. This expands robot datasets along a complementary "width" dimension--by increasing the number of actions per visited state--rather than only by collecting more trajectories. We evaluate CrowdMAPS using keyframe-centric goal-pose annotations supplied by non-expert annotators and train imitation policies on the resulting MAPS data. Across five real-world manipulation tasks, increasing MAPS width from one to ten actions per state improves sample efficiency and increases average success rates by 35.6 percentage points for keypose policies and 33.0 percentage points for trajectory policies. These results show that software-mediated human annotations can augment physical robot data to afford denser supervision, establishing CrowdMAPS as a scalable digital layer for real-robot data collection.

analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the data bottleneck in robotic imitation learning by introducing a crowdsourcing framework that augments existing robot datasets with multiple alternative actions per state. By leveraging remote human annotators via a web-based 3D interface, it increases the 'width' of the dataset without requiring additional physical robot hours, significantly improving sample efficiency and task success rates.

paper.title: Does Your World Model Know Actions Have Consequences?
paper.summary: Embodied world models (WMs) are implicit learning systems that predict the next future latent state directly from observations and actions. Unique from other end-to-end learning systems, the dynamics predictor of WMs can simulate the environment's response to alternative actions without physical deployment nor pre-specifying states of the dynamical system. Current metrics focus on the quality of model outputs, e.g., clarity of reconstructions or task success, but fail to assess the fidelity of modeling consequences of counterfactual actions. Inspecting the forced response to action perturbations through sensitivity analysis is one way to audit how well WMs can predict the consequences of counterfactual actions. Deploying WMs on hardware will require new evaluation frameworks to analyze the tradeoffs between state error and accurate sensitivity prediction.

paper.title: AMARA: Compiler-Driven Accelerator Architecture Design for Graphical Probabilistic Sampling
paper.summary: Sampling methods are fundamental primitives for training and inference on probabilistic models. However, practical deployment of sampling algorithms such as Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) remains difficult on general-purpose processors. Existing hardware accelerators improve sampling efficiency, but they are typically specialized for a narrow class of models, graph topologies, or update schedules, making it difficult to support the diverse workloads used in real applications. This paper presents AMARA, an end-to-end compiler-driven accelerator framework for probabilistic sampling on arbitrary probabilistic graphical models. AMARA introduces MCMC-IR, a domain-specific intermediate representation that separates local factorized computation from global update dependencies. Based on this representation, the compiler performs architecture-aware partitioning, scheduling, and memory-access optimization to expose parallelism and reduce irregular graph communication. The optimized program is lowered to a compact ISA and executed on a programmable ASIC accelerator with specialized compute, sampling, and memory support. By co-designing the compiler and the architecture, AMARA bridges the gap between model generality and accelerator efficiency for practical MCMC-based probabilistic computing. We evaluate AMARA across representative workloads with different structures, including grid-structured and irregular energy-based models, and causal inference networks. The results show that AMARA supports a broad spectrum of discrete probabilistic models while achieving high sampling throughput and efficient hardware utilization. AMARA achieves an average of 6.1$\times$ (up to 16.3$\times$) higher sampling throughput than a JAX-GPU baseline on irregular workloads, and offers broader programmability than state-of-the-art accelerators.

analysis.executive_summary: AMARA addresses the scalability and efficiency gap in probabilistic computing by introducing an end-to-end compiler-driven framework that co-designs software and hardware for arbitrary probabilistic graphical models. By decoupling local computation from global dependencies via a new intermediate representation, it enables efficient execution of diverse MCMC workloads on a programmable ASIC, offering a more flexible and performant alternative to both general-purpose GPUs and rigid specialized accelerators.

paper.title: Janus: One Agent, Two Roles for Digital Twin Construction and Network Orchestration
paper.summary: Next-generation wireless networks are increasingly large-scale, heterogeneous, and dynamic, posing significant challenges to network modeling and control. Digital twins offer a promising solution, but existing approaches typically rely on static models and decouple twin construction from network orchestration, limiting adaptability. Meanwhile, large language models (LLMs) provide strong reasoning capabilities but struggle with graph-structured data and are highly sensitive to prompt design, making inference unreliable. In this paper, we propose Janus, an agentic LLM-based framework that unifies digital twin construction and network orchestration within a closed-loop system. At the core of Janus is a novel NetTwin agent, which introduces a new one-agent, two-role paradigm, enabling a single agent to simultaneously construct the digital twin from partial observations while performing task-driven network decision-making. To realize this, we design a modular architecture with three functional roles, including planner, modeler, and coder, along with a newly designed unified prompt module that further enhances graph reasoning robustness. Extensive evaluations on wireless networks with up to 200 nodes and two representative tasks, including user association and SAGIN routing, show that Janus achieves over 90% digital twin accuracy and near-optimal performance with gaps within 10.53%, while maintaining moderate computational overhead. These results demonstrate the effectiveness, scalability, and generalizability of Janus, paving the way for AI-native autonomous wireless network orchestration.
